target: General SWE / backend software engineering internships (big tech + strong startups), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
bullet_feedback.problem: "the Claude skill" is referenced with a definite article before the resume ever says what it is; the reader only learns there is an AI workflow generator in the next bullet. The sentence also opens with a 15-word 'Because...' clause, so the action ('precomputed') is the 16th word.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A hiring manager reading top-down hits an undefined system and has to re-read after the third bullet to understand what this cache serves. The design decision (precompute + cache around a rate-limited table) is good, but it lands second-hand.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what 'the Claude skill' is (the AI workflow generator from the next bullet) at first mention
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Reorder the Capital One bullets so the AI workflow generator is introduced before this one, or name it here ('the AI workflow generator'); move the access-limit constraint after the action, e.g. 'Precomputed popular workflows into a category tree the AI generator searches first, and cached full workflows in Redis, because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL table had strict access limits'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Co-founded a 110+ member student product studio that has shipped 5 live products, and personally built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for one, Tortuga, a class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days
bullet_feedback.problem: The bullet stacks three separate claims (studio size, 5 products, Tortuga traffic) and the only thing labeled 'personally built' is Redis caching, whose effect is never stated. The 20,000+ visits number sits right next to the caching, so it reads as if it were the caching's result.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The candidate's own contribution is the weakest-specified part of the bullet; a HM will ask 'what did the cache change?' and 'what did you build in the other 4 products?', and the 20,000 visits figure risks looking borrowed from the team.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: why the cache was needed (load, latency, DB cost) or what changed after it; what the candidate's role in the studio's other products was, if any
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Separate the founder/studio claim from the engineering claim, and state the reason for the cache (e.g. traffic spike at registration) so the 20,000+ visits reads as the load context rather than the outcome of caching.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Deployed a space-topic research tool for Amazon Leo's public-policy team and set it up for handoff with AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code and GitHub Actions CI/CD, so Leo engineers new to the project now maintain it on AWS Fargate
bullet_feedback.problem: "space-topic research tool" does not say what the tool does, and "Deployed" leaves it ambiguous whether the candidate built it or only shipped/packaged it. Most of the bullet's words go to the handoff tooling rather than the product.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the lead bullet of a client engagement; the reader can't tell what the policy team uses it for or how much of the system is the candidate's work. The handoff outcome (Leo engineers maintain it) is genuinely strong but is attached to a vague subject.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the tool does for the policy team in a few words, and whether the candidate built it or deployed a team-built tool
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Replace 'space-topic research tool' with a short functional description, and use a verb that matches actual ownership (built / led / deployed).

bullet_feedback.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project targeting ICLR, built a Python pipeline that draws AnyGrasp candidates from multi-camera images as Open3D overlays and tuned prompts so a vision-language model picks the right grasp more often
bullet_feedback.problem: "picks the right grasp more often" is a result with no anchor, and 'draws AnyGrasp candidates ... as Open3D overlays' is hard for a non-robotics reader to parse (it is not clear that drawing overlays is how the VLM is shown the choices).
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A HM can't tell whether this moved the research result or was a minor tweak, and a recruiter can't restate the mechanism. 'More often' with no number is the kind of claim that invites a skeptical follow-up.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: how much more often (if a measurement exists), or else what the pipeline enabled for the project
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Make the mechanism explicit in plain words (render candidate grasps as overlays so the VLM can choose among them); if no measurement exists, end on what the pipeline enabled rather than an unquantified 'more often'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Automated retraining for a production Amazon Bedrock model that sorts research documents by importance: on an EventBridge schedule a larger LLM grades it, and it is fine-tuned only when those grades shift past a threshold
bullet_feedback.problem: Two pronouns 'it' after the colon are ambiguous: 'a larger LLM grades it' could mean grades the model, its outputs, or the documents. The design (drift-triggered fine-tuning judged by a stronger model) is good but takes two reads.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is one of the more interesting ML-infra decisions on the page and the reader may skim past it because the second clause doesn't parse on first read.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the larger LLM grades (the model's rankings)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Replace the pronouns with nouns, e.g. 'a larger LLM grades the model's rankings on an EventBridge schedule, and the model is fine-tuned only when those grades drift past a threshold'.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Building a RAG meal-suggestion feature for the official UMD app (GPT-4o mini, ChromaDB + SentenceBERT search); 93% of generated meals rated satisfactory by internal testers
bullet_feedback.problem: Tech-dump parenthetical plus a semicolon splice: the parenthetical lists three components without saying what any of them do, and the semicolon makes the bullet read like notes rather than a sentence.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Hurts human voice and plain-language restatability; the stack names add no engineering decision here and duplicate the Skills section.
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Turn the parenthetical into a clause only if it explains the design (e.g. what is retrieved and from where), otherwise cut it to the Skills section; replace the semicolon with a full sentence clause.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Rebuilt the legacy tool developers use to create test-data workflows as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation, and 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred it
bullet_feedback.problem: Ownership and shipping status are implicit: it is unclear if this was a solo rebuild or a team effort, and whether it replaced the legacy tool or was only piloted. 'preferred it' lacks its comparison ('over the legacy tool').
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: For an intern, 'rebuilt the legacy tool' is a large scope claim; a HM will want to know whether it is in use. The four tech names in the middle also push the result to the end of a long line.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: solo vs team, and whether developers now use it in place of the legacy tool
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Say 'preferred it over the old tool' and, if true, state that it replaced the legacy tool; trim the tech list to the pieces that explain the design (visual editor, validation).

bullet_feedback.bullet: Cut research-environment setup time 30% with uv dependency pinning and Docker, and added psutil time and memory profiling and Pytest unit tests to help the team find bottlenecks
bullet_feedback.problem: Two unrelated tasks joined by 'and', and the second ends at intent ('to help the team find bottlenecks') with no indication bottlenecks were found or fixed.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: Minor: reads as a hygiene list and is the least memorable bullet in a section that otherwise shows research engineering.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the profiling surfaced a bottleneck that was then addressed
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Either split focus to the setup-time win alone or, if the profiling found something concrete, name it; otherwise consider cutting the second clause.

page_feedback.problem: The single strongest systems evidence (IEX order book: 50.9M-message replay, 99,122/99,123 fills, 1.26M events/sec, B+ tree vs LSM comparison) sits at the bottom of the page under Projects, below eight LLM/AI-application bullets.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The intended profile is 'systems-oriented engineer'; a skimming backend HM sees Claude skills, Bedrock, RAG, and VLM prompts first and may file the candidate as an AI-app builder before reaching the systems work.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Consider tightening or cutting the weakest AI bullets (RAG meal feature, setup-time bullet) so Projects rises higher on the page, or reorder bullets within roles to lead with the infrastructure/performance work (Kinesis latency, caching, CDK handoff).

page_feedback.problem: The AWS role, the most recognizable brand and the top entry, has one bullet and no result (results intentionally omitted), so the headline role carries less evidence than every role below it.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Fine for an in-progress internship, but the 7-second skim lands on a role with the least content; the systems story has to be found further down.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep as is if nothing more can be said truthfully; make sure the single bullet front-loads the design choice (capacity bounds policy + backtesting) rather than 'Writing Java logic'.

page_feedback.problem: Ownership verbs are uneven across team projects: 'Deployed', 'Rebuilt', 'Co-founded ... personally built', 'For a PhD-led ... project, built'.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A HM screening for independent delivery can't consistently tell what was the candidate's own work versus the team's; 'personally built' on one bullet implies the others may not be.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Use verbs that accurately mark scope on each bullet (built / led / contributed X to a team Y) so ownership is legible without qualifiers.

keep: Built a C++17 order book and matching engine and replayed 50.9M real IEX exchange messages through it without ever resyncing to the exchange's book, matching 99,122 of 99,123 fills and 100% of top-of-book prices

Compared B+ tree and LSM skip-list storage for the engine's event logs on identical 2M-record workloads: the B+ tree read 12.8x faster and answered range queries 22x faster, at the cost of 27% more disk
Sustained 1.26M events/sec end-to-end over the full replay, with price levels in a std::map of FIFO queues and a hash map from order ID to queue position for O(1) cancels
Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda

Cut AI workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting one large Claude skill into smaller sub-skills that call Python tools for search and validation, after CloudWatch and OpenSearch latency logs showed where time went
Single-page layout, education-first header with grad date, and the Technical Skills section grouped by category
